title: Sleeping tendencies
hook: even a baby carries the tendencies to view, doubt and desire, asleep

segments.voice: Yesterday: the undeclared, ten questions the Buddha set aside, and the poisoned arrow. Did one question stay open while you did the next useful thing? Day four hundred fifty-six.

A baby asleep on its back, arms flung up, completely at peace. No opinions. No grudges. No wanting anything except, eventually, milk. If anyone is free of the troubles of the mind, surely it's this tiny person. The same monk from yesterday, Māluṅkyāputta, shows up again in the very next sutta. The Buddha asks the monks to recite five fetters, five things that bind a person. Māluṅkyāputta recites them perfectly. And the Buddha isn't pleased. He brings up the baby.
screen: `A BABY ASLEEP.` → `NO OPINIONS, NO GRUDGES.` → `FIVE FETTERS, RECITED PERFECTLY.`

segments.voice: The five are the lower fetters, in this sutta's list: the view that there's a fixed self, doubt, clinging to rules and rituals, sensual desire and ill will. Māluṅkyāputta has the list right. What he's missing is how deep it goes. Wanderers of other sects, the Buddha says, could refute you with one simple picture. Look at a young, tender infant lying on its back. It doesn't even have the idea of a self. How could a self-view arise in it? It has no notion of teachings, so how could it doubt them? It has no notion of rules, no notion of pleasures, no notion of other beings to resent. And yet, he says, the underlying tendency to each of these lies within it. The Pali word is anusaya, from a root meaning to lie down along with. It's the thing lying asleep under the surface. That's the turn in this sutta. A fetter isn't only what you're doing right now. You can be calm, kind, unbothered this afternoon, and the tendency to anger is still asleep in you, waiting for the right provocation. Patient all week, and then someone takes the parking spot. The sutta isn't saying babies are bad. It's saying the roots are older than our opinions. Which is why, later in the same sutta, the Buddha describes a practice that goes below the surface: settling the mind deeply and seeing how everything in it changes. A tendency you've watched wake up is one you can begin to know.
screen: `THE FIVE LOWER FETTERS.` · `A TENDER INFANT ON ITS BACK.` · `ANUSAYA: LYING ASLEEP BENEATH.` · `CALM TODAY, STILL THERE.` · then, large: `IT SLEEPS IN US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch one tendency stir. Sit and settle. Bring to mind something small that usually irritates you: a slow line, a certain tone of voice, a notification. Hold the picture just long enough to feel the first flicker, a tightening in the chest or the jaw. That flicker is a tendency waking up. Don't feed it and don't fight it. Just watch it, and watch it settle. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Sleeping tendencies. The anusayas: roots of view, doubt, desire and ill will that lie asleep in us, even in a baby, until something wakes them. Today's word.
Your line: it sleeps in us. Today, when you feel a flicker of irritation or wanting, say quietly: there it is, waking up. Day four hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: In Theravada teaching the five lower fetters and the underlying tendencies are taught as part of the stages of awakening, and meditators are trained to notice how irritation or desire arise before acting on them.

myth: the sutta says babies are wicked
it says the roots are older than our opinions, not that infants are bad.
Māluṅkyāputta got the list of five fetters wrong
he recited them correctly; the Buddha corrects his shallow grasp of them.
a tendency can be present even when it isn't active
the infant has no notion of a self, yet the tendency to self-view lies within it.

fork.setup: you've been calm and kind all week. does that mean the tendency to anger is gone?
options: not necessarily: it may be asleep
fork.reveal: the sutta's point: a tendency can lie asleep, like the ones in the infant, until something wakes it.

original.note: Pali anusaya: underlying tendency, from a root meaning to lie down along with.

trapdoor: what you thought: tendencies are habits you can see.
what it means: roots of self-view, doubt, desire and ill will lie asleep in us, even in a baby, until something wakes them.
what a scholar hears: MN 64, the Mahāmāluṅkya Sutta; anusaya, often 'latent tendency', became a major topic in Abhidhamma and in later debates between schools.

notes: MN 64 paraphrased; check the list of five lower fetters and the infant simile.
Etymology of anusaya (anu + root 'to lie') is standard but please confirm the phrasing 'to lie down along with'.
'Other teachers would laugh at your answer' renders the Buddha's remark that wanderers of other sects would confute Māluṅkyāputta with the infant simile; check.
The outline's 'view, doubt and desire' is expanded to all five fetters named in the sutta.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'other teachers would laugh at your answer' corrected to MN 64's point that wanderers of other sects could refute him with the infant simile; cut 'Most people know this already' (unsourced claim about the listener).
